one_liner: Header-only C++20 JSON library that binds to registered structs; 1.1-1.8x simdjson ondemand read throughput on most whole documents.
what_it_does: Parses JSON straight into C++ structs and serializes them back; you register each struct by specializing jsonifier::core<T> with a list of member pointers (createValue<&T::a, makeJsonEntity<&T::b, "b-key">()>()), with no macros or code generation. You call parser.parseJson<parse_options{...}>(obj, buf) or serializeJson on a reusable jsonifier_core<> object, which returns bool and puts errors in getErrors() instead of throwing. It is not a drop-in for simdjson: there is no DOM or On-Demand cursor API, only raw_json_data, a lazily built variant tree for subtrees with no fixed schema. It also validates, minifies and prettifies raw JSON.
how_it_is_fast: A full-document parse skips simdjson-style stage-1 structural indexing and makes one schema-guided pass over the raw bytes, comparing each member header against a key literal built at compile time (with minified+knownOrder, `,"key":` is a single fixed-length compare). When keys arrive out of order it falls back to a hash-map dispatch generated at compile time for that struct's exact key set, and a thread_local per-type table learns the observed order so the next document takes the fast path. UTF-8 is validated only over string bytes, inside the SIMD string-unescape loop, and the ISA is fixed at compile time, so there is no runtime dispatch. The Langdale-Lemire stage-1 index (clmul prefix-XOR, batched tzcnt drain, VBMI2 compress on AVX-512) runs only for partialRead, minify and prettify.
when_to_use: Deserializing stable, known schemas (API responses, protocol messages, log records) into C++ structs where you would otherwise hand-write simdjson ondemand traversal. The largest whole-document gains are on minified input, e.g. Twitter minified 2116 vs 1212 MB/s and Instruments minified 3335 vs 1476 MB/s.
Many tiny documents parsed one at a time, like single scalars or small messages. With no per-document stage-1 setup, the authors measured 2.4-13.7x over ondemand on files of single-value documents.
Producers that emit keys in a different order than your struct declares. The learned key-order table avoids ondemand's forward rescans: Marine IK Reverse minified reads at 810 vs 191 MB/s.

You also want fast typed writes, minify and prettify from the same library. simdjson has no struct serializer, and on the Clang page Jsonifier's writes beat Glaze in most tests (Twitter minified write 7689 vs 5868 MB/s).
Server builds where you control the target CPU at compile time (-march=native style): x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512, or aarch64 with NEON.
when_not_to_use: Schemas only known at runtime, or exploratory traversal. raw_json_data is the fallback, and the docs say it is slower than registered structs. The authors' own design paper names simdjson DOM/On-Demand as the right tool for dynamic workloads.

GCC builds reading pretty-printed input. On the authors' Linux/GCC 16.1 page, simdjson ondemand wins Twitter prettified (2266 vs 1802 MB/s), Mesh prettified (2241 vs 1549), Random prettified (1701 vs 1367), and CitmCatalog and Canada prettified. The authors' own tally for Linux/GCC is 18 wins, 1 tie and 12 losses against simdjson.

Portable binaries for CPUs you don't know in advance. The SIMD backend is fixed when you configure with no runtime dispatch, so a wrong JSONIFIER_CPU_INSTRUCTIONS gives SIGILL or a silent scalar fallback. The vcpkg port does not support Windows ARM, Xbox or 32-bit targets.
ARM SVE2 targets. That backend is marked experimental with known incorrect parsing cases, and NEON is the recommended production path.

Teams that need a mature, widely reviewed dependency. It has one listed contributor, 103 stars and v1.0.0 only in June 2026. Past ASan-found string over-reads (issues #27 and #30) were fixed. The docs contradict each other on some defaults: validateUtf8 is listed as false in one page but defaults to true in config.hpp, and the minimum Clang is 14 in one page and 16 in another. Glaze also beats it on Discord and Google Maps minified reads.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (fast_float code is vendored in-tree); the unit tests fetch rt-ut via CMake FetchContent
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; README lists MSVC 2022+, GCC 11+ and Clang 16+ (Installation.md says Clang 14+); CMake 3.28+. The INTERFACE target raises the constexpr evaluation limits (-fconstexpr-steps=100000000 on Clang, -fconstexpr-ops-limit=1000000000 on GCC, /constexpr:steps100000000 on MSVC)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (scalar, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 with F+BW+VBMI2) and aarch64 NEON; SVE2 experimental; CI runs on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows; Android is best-effort
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. In the source, a jsonifier_core instance holds mutable scratch buffers and the error list, so use one per thread. The per-type knownOrder tables and root-array scratch vectors are thread_local, so instances on different threads do not share parse state.

gotchas: nullTerminated defaults to true, so the parser relies on a '\0' after the buffer and skips bounds checks. Passing std::vector<char> or a raw file/socket buffer without a trailing NUL is undefined behavior unless you set nullTerminated=false.

minified=true is a promise about the input: whitespace then causes parse failures. The published benchmark runs Jsonifier with knownOrder=true and minified set to match each file, so measure with the flags your input actually guarantees.

The build depends on CMake. Configure runs a CPU probe and writes include/jsonifier-incl/simd/jsonifier_cpu_instructions.hpp into the source tree (the checked-in copy hard-codes 111 = AVX2+BMI+CLMUL). The JSONIFIER_PLATFORM_*/COMPILER_*/INLINE macros are also CMake compile definitions, so copying the headers in by hand means defining all of them yourself. Include only <jsonifier>: internal headers #define reinterpret_cast, const_cast, dynamic_cast and memcpy to static_assert traps.

A default jsonifier_core<> allocates a 1 MB string buffer plus a 1M-entry uint32 tape (about 5 MB), possibly on huge pages, so reuse one per thread instead of constructing one per call. The string_view returned by serializeJson(data) is invalidated by the next parse or serialize call on that instance.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you work in C++, your incumbent is simdjson, and you want typed struct binding with compile-time reflection plus serialization. LJSON and zzzJSON are benchmarked only against RapidJSON, and simd-json, jiter, Sonic, go-json, jsoniter and easyjson serve Rust or Go, not C++.
verified_claims_summary: In the authors' own Json-Performance harness (Clang 24.0.0, -O3 -march=native -flto=thin, AVX2 backend vs simdjson haswell, i9-14900KF under WSL2, UTF-8 validation on for all libraries), Jsonifier reads into typed structs were 2.4-13.7x faster than simdjson ondemand on files of tiny single-value documents. On most whole documents the gain was about 1.1-1.75x (e.g. Twitter minified 2116 vs 1212 MB/s), with statistical ties on Twitter, Google Maps and Random prettified and a loss on Mesh prettified (1919 vs 2113 MB/s); Jsonifier ran with knownOrder=true and minified set to match the input, options ondemand has no equivalent for.
status_note: Actively developed by a single maintainer (v1.0.2 released 2026-09-22, CI green on main), MIT-licensed and packaged in vcpkg; it is header-only but should be consumed through its CMake target rather than copied in by hand.
